abstract: It is known that any two-outcome quantum measurement can be decomposed into a continuous stochastic process using a feedback loop. In this article, we characterize which of these decompositions are possible when each iteration of the feedback loop consists of a weak measurement caused by an interaction with a probe system. We restrict ourselves to the case when the probe is a qubit and the interaction Hamiltonian between the probe and system is constant. We find that even given the ability to perform arbitrary unitary pulses throughout the continuous decomposition, only generalized measurements with two distinct singular values are achievable. However, this is sufficient to decompose a generalized qubit measurement using a qubit probe and a simple interaction Hamiltonian.

specification.problem: Decompose a two-outcome generalized quantum measurement {M_0, M_1} on a system into a continuous (many-step) stochastic sequence of weak measurements, where each weak measurement is realized by coupling the system to a fresh qubit probe through a constant interaction Hamiltonian for a short time and then projectively measuring the probe, with classical feedback deciding when to stop (and, in general, which unitary pulses to apply). The abstract claims that with a qubit probe and constant Hamiltonian only measurements whose Kraus operator has two distinct singular values are reachable, which suffices for arbitrary two-outcome qubit measurements.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest useful instance (chosen here as an assumption, no experiment_scope supplied): system = 1 qubit, probe = 1 qubit, constant interaction H = g Z_S \otimes Y_P applied for time dt (weak-coupling angle \varepsilon = g\,dt \ll 1), probe prepared in |0\rangle and read out in the X basis each iteration. The target is a diagonal two-outcome qubit measurement M_0 = diag(cos\theta, sin\theta), M_1 = diag(sin\theta, cos\theta) with a tiny explicit choice \theta = \pi/8, \varepsilon = 0.05. The stochastic decomposition is a random walk on the measurement angle \Theta_n with a stopping rule; no intermediate unitary pulses are needed for this diagonal target. Outside scope: the paper's full characterization theorem (proof that exactly two distinct singular values are reachable for arbitrary system dimension), the role of arbitrary unitary pulses between iterations, non-diagonal/non-commuting targets, higher-dimensional systems, and the paper's specific feedback law.

equations.label: Target two-outcome measurement (instance)
equations.latex: M_0 = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & \sin\theta \end{pmatrix},\quad M_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix},\quad M_0^\dagger M_0 + M_1^\dagger M_1 = I
equations.description: Completeness relation for a two-outcome measurement and the explicit diagonal qubit target used in the scoped instance; each Kraus operator has two distinct singular values (cos\theta, sin\theta) for \theta \ne \pi/4.
equations.justification: Completeness is standard; the specific diagonal form is a chosen tiny instance of a 'generalized qubit measurement' with two distinct singular values, consistent with the abstract's claimed achievable class.
assumptions: Target chosen diagonal in the Z basis so that all weak Kraus operators commute and no unitary pulses are needed

equations.label: Weak measurement via constant-Hamiltonian probe interaction
equations.latex: U = e^{-i H\, dt},\qquad K_m = (I_S \otimes \langle m|_P)\, U\, (I_S \otimes |0\rangle_P),\qquad \sum_m K_m^\dagger K_m = I_S
equations.description: One iteration of the feedback loop: a fresh probe in |0\rangle interacts with the system under the constant Hamiltonian H for time dt, then the probe is projectively measured in basis {|m\rangle}; the induced system Kraus operators K_m form a weak measurement.
equations.abstract_quote: each iteration of the feedback loop consists of a weak measurement caused by an interaction with a probe system
equations.justification: The abstract states each iteration is a weak measurement induced by a probe interaction with a constant Hamiltonian; the Stinespring/indirect-measurement form is the standard way such an interaction yields system Kraus operators. The probe initial state |0\rangle and readout basis are not specified in the abstract.
assumptions: Probe is initialized in a fixed pure state (taken as |0\rangle) and measured projectively each step
Probe is discarded/reset after every iteration

equations.label: Instance Kraus operators for H = g Z\otimes Y with X-basis probe readout
equations.latex: e^{-i\varepsilon Z\otimes Y}|0\rangle_P = \cos\varepsilon\, I\otimes|0\rangle + \sin\varepsilon\, Z\otimes|1\rangle,\qquad K_\pm = \frac{\cos\varepsilon\, I \pm \sin\varepsilon\, Z}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\mp\varepsilon) & 0 \\ 0 & \sin(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\mp\varepsilon) \end{pmatrix}
equations.description: Explicit weak-measurement Kraus operators for the chosen Hamiltonian, probe readout in the X eigenbasis |\pm\rangle = (|0\rangle \pm |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}. Each K_\pm is a weak Z-measurement with two distinct singular values; K_+^\dagger K_+ + K_-^\dagger K_- = I holds exactly.
equations.justification: Direct evaluation of eq_2 for the chosen H using (Z\otimes Y)^2 = I and Y|0\rangle = i|1\rangle; the Hamiltonian choice is a proposed 'simple interaction Hamiltonian', not taken from the paper.
assumptions: Probe measured in the X basis (Hadamard then computational readout)

equations.label: Accumulated Kraus operator after n commuting weak steps
equations.description: Because all K_\pm are diagonal, the product after n steps is exactly a positive scalar times a diagonal operator of the same two-singular-value form; the angle \Theta_n performs a random walk on (0,\pi/2) starting at \Theta_0 = \pi/4, moving towards 0 on '+' and towards \pi/2 on '-'. Equivalently \log\tan\Theta_n = n_+\log\tan(\pi/4-\varepsilon) + n_-\log\tan(\pi/4+\varepsilon), a symmetric-step walk since \tan(\pi/4-\varepsilon)\tan(\pi/4+\varepsilon)=1.
equations.justification: Exact algebraic consequence of eq_3 (commuting diagonal matrices); the exact equality holds for every path, with c_n = \sqrt{\cos^2\Theta_n'+\sin^2\Theta_n'} absorbing the overall scale (not written out).
assumptions: Only valid for the diagonal (commuting) instance; non-commuting targets would require the unitary pulses mentioned in the abstract

equations.label: Feedback stopping rule and approximation of the target
equations.latex: T = \min\{n : \Theta_n \le \theta \ \text{or}\ \Theta_n \ge \tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\},\qquad \text{outcome } 0 \text{ if } \Theta_T \le \theta,\ 1 \text{ if } \Theta_T \ge \tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta;\qquad \sum_{\text{paths}\to 0} K^{(T)\dagger}K^{(T)} \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\to 0\ } M_0^\dagger M_0
equations.description: Classical feedback: continue weak steps until the accumulated angle crosses either threshold, then declare the corresponding outcome. Each stopped path gives K^{(T)} \propto diag(cos\Theta_T, sin\Theta_T) with \Theta_T within one step (O(\varepsilon)) of \theta or \pi/2-\theta, so the resulting Kraus operator equals the target only up to a scalar and an overshoot of order \varepsilon; the equality to M_0^\dagger M_0 is a continuous-limit approximation, not exact at finite \varepsilon.
equations.justification: Random-walk-with-stopping decomposition of a two-outcome measurement into weak measurements is the known construction (Oreshkov–Brun type) referred to by the abstract's first sentence; the specific thresholds are our proposal for this instance. Convergence is recalled from background knowledge, not verified here.
assumptions: Stopping-time feedback is the only feedback used; no unitary pulses
The limit statement is an approximation in \varepsilon with unverified rate
Path probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to K^{(T)} on the actual system state, which the stopping rule respects because K_\pm are trace-preserving-complete at every step

equations.label: Two-singular-value constraint on achievable measurements
equations.latex: M_0 = V\,\big(s_1 P + s_2 (I-P)\big)\,W,\qquad s_1 \ne s_2 \in [0,1],\quad V, W \text{ unitary},\ P^2 = P = P^\dagger
equations.description: Characterization claimed by the abstract: with a qubit probe and constant Hamiltonian, even with arbitrary unitary pulses, the decomposable two-outcome measurements are exactly those whose Kraus operator has at most two distinct singular values (singular value decomposition with a two-valued spectrum). For a qubit system (d=2) this is no restriction, which is the sufficiency claim.
equations.abstract_quote: only generalized measurements with two distinct singular values are achievable
equations.justification: The abstract explicitly states the two-distinct-singular-values constraint; the SVD form is the standard way to write that condition. The proof and the precise handling of degenerate cases (s_1 = s_2, zero singular values) are not available from the abstract.
assumptions: Interpretation of 'two distinct singular values' as the singular spectrum of M_0 taking at most two values; the paper's exact statement (e.g., whether M_1 is constrained identically via M_1^\dagger M_1 = I - M_0^\dagger M_0) is not verifiable here

registers.name: S
registers.role: System qubit carrying the state to be measured; persists through all iterations

registers.name: P
registers.role: Probe qubit, prepared in |0\rangle at the start of every iteration, coupled via H, measured in the X basis, then reset/discarded

registers.name: c
registers.size: classical: running integers n_+, n_- (or the real \Theta_n)
registers.role: Classical feedback record used to evaluate the stopping rule

specification.initial_state: |\psi\rangle_S \otimes |0\rangle_P with arbitrary system qubit state |\psi\rangle (tensor order S \otimes P, i.e., basis |s\rangle_S|p\rangle_P with s the first/most-significant bit); classical counters n_+ = n_- = 0, \Theta_0 = \pi/4.

steps.description: Reset the probe to |0\rangle_P (fresh probe for iteration n+1).
Apply the constant-Hamiltonian interaction U = exp(-i \varepsilon Z_S \otimes Y_P) for one time step dt (\varepsilon = g\,dt), entangling system and probe.
Measure the probe in the X basis (apply Hadamard to P, then measure P in the computational basis); record outcome m \in \{+,-\}. The system undergoes Kraus operator K_m.
Classically update n_+ or n_- and the accumulated angle \Theta_n via tan\Theta_n = tan^{n_+}(\pi/4-\varepsilon) tan^{n_-}(\pi/4+\varepsilon).

Evaluate the stopping rule: if \Theta_n \le \theta declare outcome 0; if \Theta_n \ge \pi/2-\theta declare outcome 1; otherwise return to step 1. The declared outcome realizes the target measurement eq_1 approximately (exactly in the \varepsilon \to 0 limit), and the overall construction stays within the two-singular-value class of eq_6.

specification.measurement: Only the probe qubit P is measured, once per iteration, in the X eigenbasis (Hadamard followed by Z-basis readout). The system qubit is never directly measured; its post-measurement state is K^{(T)}|\psi\rangle / \|K^{(T)}|\psi\rangle\|. For the explicit instance (\theta=\pi/8, \varepsilon=0.05) the walk in \log\tan\Theta_n has step size 2\,\mathrm{artanh}... more precisely |\log\tan(\pi/4\pm 0.05)| \approx 0.1003 and must travel |\log\tan(\pi/8)| \approx 0.8814, so roughly 9 or more iterations are needed before stopping.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Maintain counters (n_+, n_-), compute \Theta_n, apply the two-threshold stopping rule of eq_5, and output the binary outcome. Optionally verify the decomposition statistically by comparing the empirical outcome-0 frequency over many runs with \langle\psi|M_0^\dagger M_0|\psi\rangle = \cos^2\theta\,|\psi_0|^2 + \sin^2\theta\,|\psi_1|^2, expecting agreement only up to O(\varepsilon) overshoot bias.
assumptions: No experiment_scope was provided; the single-qubit system, Z\otimes Y Hamiltonian, |0\rangle probe preparation, X-basis probe readout, \theta = \pi/8 and \varepsilon = 0.05 are all chosen here, not taken from the paper

The target measurement is diagonal so that weak Kraus operators commute and the abstract's 'arbitrary unitary pulses' are not needed; this sidesteps the general (non-commuting) case the paper addresses
The stopping-time feedback rule is a standard random-walk construction and may differ from the paper's feedback law

Convergence of the stopped-walk effect to M_0^\dagger M_0 as \varepsilon \to 0 is recalled from background knowledge and not verified; at finite \varepsilon the realized Kraus operator deviates from the target by a scalar and an O(\varepsilon) angle overshoot
Register ordering S \otimes P with the system as the first tensor factor
